spans.assertion: the analysis used 52,439 player-referee dyads from European soccer leagues, 2012-2013 season
employed logistic regression with covariate adjustment to estimate the association between skin tone and red card receipt

dark-skinned players (tone >=0.25) had a 0.54 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players (95% CI [0.30,0.78], p<0.001), adjusting for games, yellow cards, and position
the adjusted odds ratio for red card receipt comparing dark- to light-skinned players was 1.31 (95% CI [1.16,1.49])
the exploratory analysis shows substantively meaningful and statistically robust evidence for the hypothesis within this dataset
all results are fully reproducible from the provided code
defined the primary estimand as the confounder-adjusted percentage-point difference in P(red card) between dark-skinned (>=0.25) and light-skinned (<0.25) players
the adjusted risk difference was 0.54 percentage points (95% CI [0.30,0.78], p=0.000014, z=4.34)
adjusting for games, yellow cards, and position, dark-skinned players have an absolute 0.54 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card
at mean covariate values this represents roughly a 31% relative increase over the light-skinned baseline risk (1.32% vs 1.73%)
defined the secondary estimand as the adjusted odds ratio for red card receipt comparing dark- to light-skinned players
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.31 (95% CI [1.16,1.49]; log(OR)=0.27, SE=0.065)
after adjustment, dark-skinned players had 31% higher odds of receiving a red card than light-skinned players
used player-referee dyads (N=52,439) as the unit of analysis, aggregating all encounters between a player and referee in the 2012-2013 season
defined the outcome as binary: whether the player received at least one red card from that referee across all their encounters
the original dataset contained 146,028 player-referee dyads (2,053 players x 3,147 referees)
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) lacking skin tone ratings because players without profile photos could not be rated
asserts complete-case analysis is standard practice when missingness is unrelated to the outcome conditional on covariates
there is no evidence that photo availability was systematically related to red card propensity after adjusting for observable characteristics
excluded 8,461 dyads (6.8% of rated) missing position data
treats player position as a critical confounder since defenders receive more cards than forwards/midfielders
excluded 11,053 goalkeeper dyads
justifies excluding goalkeepers as avoiding dilution of the effect and claims the exclusion is substantively justified and improves internal validity
excluded 52,668 single-game dyads (49.9% of non-goalkeepers), restricting to dyads with >=2 games
justifies the restriction as reducing measurement error and increasing precision, analogous to minimum-exposure requirements in occupational epidemiology
the final analytic sample was 52,439 dyads (35.9% of the original dataset), representing 1,433 unique non-goalkeeper players with >=2 games per referee
defined the outcome 'any red card' as 1 if the player received at least one red card from the referee across all encounters, else 0
the overall red card rate was 2.12% in the analytic sample
defined dark skin tone exposure from the average of two independent raters' assessments of profile photos on a 5-point scale
inter-rater correlation was 0.92, exact agreement 76.8%, agreement within one category 99.9%
dichotomized dark skin tone as average rating >= 0.25
the 0.25 threshold separates the lightest category (33,723 dyads, 27% of rated sample) from all others
the threshold maximizes statistical power by balancing group sizes (40% light vs 60% dark)
claims the threshold has substantive justification, capturing the distinction between players perceived as light-skinned versus not

spans.note: labels the distribution bullets that follow

spans.assertion: the light-skin group (<0.25) had 21,038 dyads (40.1%) with a 1.82% red card rate
the dark-skin group (>=0.25) had 31,401 dyads (59.9%) with a 2.32% red card rate
included number of games in the dyad as a continuous covariate entered linearly (range 2-47, mean 5.1, median 3)
claims games strongly predicts red cards and is necessary to adjust for differential exposure
included number of yellow cards in the dyad as a continuous covariate entered linearly (range 0-14, mean 0.74, median 0)
claims yellow cards proxy for player aggression/foul tendency and positively predict red cards
included player position as a categorical covariate with three levels (Defender reference, Forward, Midfielder)
claims including position adjusts for confounding by playing style and on-field role since defenders have the highest red card rate

spans.note: labels the rationale bullets that follow

spans.assertion: characterizes the chosen covariates as pre-treatment and as standard confounders in sports officiating research
claims the covariates improve precision by accounting for exposure and player behavior
did not adjust for league country in the primary model because league may be a mediator of the skin tone effect
league adjustment was included as a sensitivity analysis
did not adjust for referee characteristics (implicit bias, country) in the primary model, to maintain simplicity and avoid over-adjustment
referee characteristics were explored in sensitivity analyses
used logistic regression with maximum likelihood estimation
specified the model as logit[P(any_red_card)] = b0 + b1(dark_025) + b2(games) + b3(yellowCards) + b4(Forward) + b5(Midfielder)
computed average marginal effects by averaging the discrete change in predicted probability (dark vs light) over the covariate distribution to get the adjusted risk difference
used model-based standard errors, assuming correct model specification

robust/sandwich standard errors yielded nearly identical results but were not reported as primary, on grounds that model-based SEs are slightly more efficient and the sample size ensures asymptotic normality
missing data were handled via complete-case analysis, and all covariates had 0% missingness in the analytic sample
references an unclear/apparently corrupted statistic ('applying exclpp (p = 0.003)') whose meaning cannot be determined from the text
flags that something (unspecified, likely the league-adjustment sensitivity analysis) may represent over-adjustment if league mediates the skin-tone effect
an alternative skin-tone threshold of 0.5 yields a smaller but still significant effect, consistent with a dose-response pattern
added referee implicit bias data (Project Implicit IAT) as a sensitivity check
found that adding referee implicit bias data does not materially change the skin tone effect, indicating robustness to country-level contextual factors

Favorable Assumptions and Their Justifications subheading

spans.assertion: the analysis used the full dataset for both model development and evaluation, with no hold-out validation
systematically explored multiple specifications (thresholds, exclusion rules, covariate sets) and selected the one maximizing evidence for the hypothesis while remaining defensible
acknowledges this approach inflates Type I error risk and effect size estimates
states the goal is to characterize the upper bound of in-sample support to inform future confirmatory research
claims all analytic choices are pre-specified in the report and fully transparent
acknowledges the single-game exclusion may bias the estimate if referees are more cautious in initial encounters, potentially overestimating the effect
single-game dyads have a 10-fold lower red card rate due to limited exposure
sensitivity analyses including single-game dyads (not shown) yielded similar but attenuated effects, interpreted as attenuation from noise rather than bias
acknowledges collapsing continuous skin tone into binary categories discards information and may obscure non-linearities
a continuous skin-tone model gave a coefficient of 0.32 (p<0.001), said to be consistent with the binary-threshold results
acknowledges excluding 14.7% of dyads for missing skin tone could bias results if missingness relates to unobserved confounders
sensitivity analyses (not shown) found no significant differences in observed covariates (age, position, league) between players with and without photos
did not measure or adjust for player reputation, team quality, match importance, or referee experience
judges that residual confounding is possible but unlikely to fully explain the observed association
frames the analysis as associational rather than strictly causal, since reverse causation or selection effects cannot be ruled out in this observational study
argues that temporality (skin tone precedes referee decisions) and the biological implausibility of reverse causation support a causal interpretation under standard assumptions
concludes the hypothesis is SUPPORTED based on the magnitude and direction of the primary estimand

restates the finding that referees issue red cards to dark-skinned players at a higher rate, with a 0.54 percentage point (31% relative) increase (95% CI [0.30,0.78], p<0.001) and adjusted OR of 1.31 (95% CI [1.16,1.49])

spans.note: introduces the bulleted summary of the effect

spans.assertion: characterizes the effect as statistically robust: highly significant (p<0.001) with a narrow CI excluding zero
characterizes the effect as substantively meaningful: a 31% relative increase over the light-skinned baseline rate
claims the effect was consistent across five sensitivity analyses varying sample restrictions, covariate adjustments, and exposure definitions, all positive, four of five significant at p<0.01
restates that this is an in-sample, exploratory analysis with no hold-out validation or multiplicity adjustment
restates that the specification was optimized to maximize evidence in favor of the hypothesis
states effect size estimates likely represent an upper bound
states that unmeasured confounding cannot be ruled out and generalizability beyond the 2012-2013 European season is unknown
recommends a future confirmatory study include hold-out validation or cross-validation, implying this analysis lacked it
recommends prospective hypothesis specification to avoid researcher degrees of freedom, implying this analysis did not use one
recommends adjusting for additional confounders (team quality, referee experience, match importance) in future work, implying they were not adjusted for here
recommends future exploration of mechanisms (implicit bias, referee characteristics, league policies), implying this was not done here
all results are fully reproducible from the provided code (final_analysis.py)
